title: The Executive
hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.
key_points: The executive carries out and enforces the laws the legislature passes.
It runs the administration: ministries, agencies, the civil service, and the armed forces.
A head of state symbolizes the nation; a head of government runs policy — sometimes the same person.
Its reach makes it powerful, which is why constitutions hedge it with checks and fixed terms.
content_html: If the legislature makes the law, the executive is the branch that puts it into effect. It is the working machinery of the state: the ministries and agencies that deliver services, the civil service that administers programs, and the command of the police and armed forces. Because it acts continuously and controls vast resources, the executive is where much of the practical power of government concentrates — and where decisive action in a crisis is expected.
extra_html: Two roles often sit inside the executive. The head of state symbolizes and represents the nation as a whole — receiving ambassadors, embodying continuity — while the head of government directs actual policy and the administration. These can be separate people, as with a monarch or ceremonial president alongside a prime minister, or combined in one figure, as with a presidential system's president. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the executive's broad reach is exactly why constitutions surround it with limits: fixed terms, legislative control of budgets, judicial review of its actions, and requirements to answer for its conduct. The recurring design problem is to give the executive enough authority to govern effectively without letting that authority slip free of accountability.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: The Legislature
related.hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Civil Service & Bureaucracy
related.hook: Governments change; the bureaucracy stays. The permanent civil service is the machinery that actually delivers policy — for better and, sometimes, for worse.

flashcards.prompt: What is the executive branch's main role?
flashcards.back_html: To carry out and enforce the laws — running the administration, agencies, civil service, and armed forces day to day.

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between a head of state and a head of government?

choices.text: The head of state symbolizes the nation; the head of government runs policy
The head of state writes laws; the head of government vetoes them
They are always two different people in every country

flashcards.explanation_html: The roles can be split (e.g. a monarch and a prime minister) or combined in one person (e.g. a president), depending on the system.

flashcards.prompt: Why do constitutions typically place extra checks on the executive?

choices.text: Its control of the bureaucracy and force makes it especially powerful
It is the weakest branch and needs protection
It is the only branch that is elected

flashcards.explanation_html: Because the executive commands administration and force, constitutions hedge it with checks, fixed terms, and oversight to prevent abuse.
